Paragraph: Musing over those past events Dasaratha said, 'Sorrowing for my son, I too will die now and the curse of the sage will come to pass. Banishing Rama was an injustice and does not befit me. No greater grief can befall me than that of not seeing him. It was my destiny to banish Rama as dictated by Kaikeyi. 'If only Rama can touch me once, or appear before me, I may still live. Once a person goes to the land of the dead, they can no longer see any one. Kausalya! I cannot see you, my faculties are deserting me, and the messengers of death hurry me. My life flickers as a flame in a lamp whose oil is soon to be over, my body feels like the banks of a river, being washed away, by the force of its waters.' As death approached and drove away his hopes of ever seeing Rama, a cry of torment escaped Dasaratha who called out 'O Rama! Where are you my son and my protector?Kausalya! Sumitra! Kaikeyi you are my enemy, the destroyer of my race!' Remorseful and above all anguished beyond endurance at Rama's separation, the noble Ikshvaku Dasaratha, fated to die away fromRama, gave up the last breath of life, a little after midnight.
Situation/Problem_Faced: Dasaratha is on his deathbed, consumed by the realization that the sage's curse is coming to fruition. He experiences profound grief and sadness over Rama's absence, clinging to a desperate hope of seeing him one last time. As his physical faculties fail, he expresses his torment and despair, blaming Kaikeyi and succumbing to death, unable to bear the anguish of separation from Rama.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: The passage vividly portrays the psychological and physical deterioration leading to death, driven by overwhelming sorrow. Dasaratha's acceptance of the curse signifies his acceptance of consequences (karma). His final cries for Rama, despite his awareness of impending death, highlight the unbearable pain of unresolved loss and the intense longing for his 'protector.' His final accusation towards Kaikeyi is a manifestation of his unresolved anger and resentment.
Outcome/Resolution: Dasaratha dies, consumed by grief and anguish over Rama's separation, fulfilling the sage's curse. His death marks the tragic culmination of his past actions and their severe consequences.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Dukha (Dasaratha's ultimate state of suffering and anguish, dominating his final moments.)
Karma Phala (The explicit fulfillment of the sage's curse, directly linking his past 'sin' to his present death, confirming the inescapable nature of consequences.)
Moha (The initial delusion that led to Rama's exile, now leading to his death through grief, a cycle of suffering perpetuated by attachment and wrong action.)
Viyoga-Dukha (The suffering caused by separation from a beloved one, which is the primary cause of his death, 'anguished beyond endurance at Rama's separation.')
Mrityu (Death, as a powerful force, with its 'messengers' and the flickering of life, highlighting the end of the physical journey.)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Dasaratha's final moments are a tragic culmination of Dukha (suffering) and the explicit fulfillment of Karma Phala, as the sage's curse comes to pass. His death is directly caused by 'Viyoga-Dukha' (suffering from separation) from Rama, embodying the ultimate consequence of his past actions. Despite fleeting moments of self-blame for his 'injustice,' his final cries reflect profound spiritual anguish and the painful impact of Moha (attachment) and the Karma it set in motion, leading to a death marked by inescapable sorrow.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Dasaratha's demise is a profound portrayal of death by grief. He is consumed by sadness and feelings of hopelessness, accepting the inevitability of the curse. His desperate longing to see Rama, coupled with the fading of his faculties, highlights intense anxiety and psychological torment. His final cries of 'O Rama!' and the blame directed at Kaikeyi are expressions of his unbearable anguish and unresolved anger, showing the ultimate breakdown of his coping mechanisms. His death, 'anguished beyond endurance at Rama's separation,' is a stark illustration of how profound relationship challenges and unrelenting sorrow can lead to fatal psychological and physical collapse.
